newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian prosecutor -- from accuser to accused.
newsitem.headline: Colombian prosecutor -- from accuser to accused.

text.p: Are the chickens coming home to roost for Alfonso Valdivieso, the man who has done more than perhaps anyone before him to expose drug corruption at the highest levels of the Colombian government?
That's what many Colombians were asking on Monday after Valdivieso, the respected chief prosecutor, was accused of having received narcotics money for his personal benefit.

People like Luis Guillermo Nieto Roa, the lawyer who sucessfully defended President Ernesto Samper against the drug corruption charges Valdivieso brought against him this year, appeared anything but disappointed by the fact that the prosecutor -- a sworn enemy of corrupt politicians -- looked set to get a taste of his own medicine.
Attorney General Orlando Vasquez Velasquez accused Valdivieso on Friday of receiving more than $3,400 from a car dealership owned by a drug trafficker to finance a failed bid for the Senate in 1993.
The fact that the charge came from Vasquez, who was suspended from office this year because of his own alleged ties to drug lords, led many to dismiss it at first.

But Valdivieso conceded over the weekend that he did in fact receive a campaign contribution from the car dealership, Automotores Santa Barbara, which Vasquez said was owned by reputed drug trafficker Efrain Hernandez.

Valdivieso said the contribution was in the form of a check made out by the dealership's general manager, a personal friend he identified as Carlos Obando, and insisted he had no way of knowing Hernandez was involved.

Valdivieso, whom polls regularly show to be one of Colombia's most respected public figures, also said he would be willing to have his campaign finances investigated by a special congressional committee in a bid to clear his name.

Nieto Roa, Samper's attorney, told Reuters by telephone on Monday there was no question an investigation should be opened and it should be just as rigorous as those Valdivieso forced Samper and about 20 lawmakers to undergo, given the fact that he is the country's chief criminal investigator.

"The same rule should apply to him that he has applied to everyone else, that it's not enough to say he didn't know," Nieto Roa said of the alleged illicit financing of Valdivieso's campaign. He said Valdivieso unleashed a virtual "witch hunt" by insisting that any politician who received the slightest amount of drug-tainted money, with or without his knowledge, should be suspected of "illicit enrichment."
